abstract.title: ABSTRACT
abstract.p: Mosunetuzumab plus polatuzumab vedotin has shown promising activity versus rituximab plus polatuzumab vedotin (R‐Pola) in patients with relapsed/refractory (R/R) large B‐cell lymphoma (LBCL; NCT03671018). We present results from the Phase II randomized cohort, evaluating subcutaneous mosunetuzumab plus polatuzumab vedotin (Mosun‐Pola), with > 2 years of follow‐up. Patients with R/R LBCL and ≥ 1 prior line of therapy were randomized to receive Mosun‐Pola or R‐Pola. Mosunetuzumab was administered subcutaneously with Cycle (C) 1 step‐up dosing (5/45/45 mg) then 45 mg on C2 Day (D) 1–C8D1 (21‐day cycles). Polatuzumab vedotin (1.8 mg/kg) was given intravenously (IV) on D1 of C1–6. Rituximab IV (375 mg/m2) was given on D1 of C1–8. Primary endpoint was best objective response rate (ORR). As of November 15, 2024, 80 patients had been enrolled (Mosun‐Pola, n = 40; R‐Pola, n = 40). Best ORR was 77.5% (95% confidence interval [CI] 61.6–89.2) for Mosun‐Pola and 50.0% (95% CI: 33.8–66.2) for R‐Pola; complete response (CR) rates were 55.0% (95% CI: 38.5–70.7) and 35.0% (95% CI: 20.6–51.7), respectively. Median progression‐free survival was 25.4 months for Mosun‐Pola and 6.4 months for R‐Pola (hazard ratio [HR] 0.47); median overall survival was not reached and 25.5 months (HR: 0.78), respectively. Cytokine release syndrome occurred in 12.5% of Mosun‐Pola‐treated patients (all Grade 1/2). Fixed‐duration Mosun‐Pola demonstrated benefit across all efficacy endpoints compared with R‐Pola in patients with R/R LBCL. These findings are consistent with the observed benefit of Mosun‐Pola for patients with R/R LBCL in the global Phase III SUNMO study (NCT05171647).

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Although cure is possible for many patients with newly diagnosed large B‐cell lymphoma (LBCL) treated with rituximab‐based immunochemotherapy, approximately 20%–40% of patients have disease that is either refractory to this frontline therapy or that subsequently relapses, requiring additional treatment [1, 2, 3]. Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T‐cell therapies may be utilized as a second‐line treatment option; however, widespread adoption remains a challenge due to logistical and patient‐related hurdles [4]. Other treatment options, including bispecific antibodies, monoclonal antibody combinations, and novel chemoimmunotherapy regimens, are also available [4, 5]. Nevertheless, there remains a need for new therapies for the treatment of relapsed/refractory (R/R) LBCL that provide durable responses and curative potential while also balancing patient safety and access, especially in nontertiary and community settings where many patients receive treatment.

Mosunetuzumab is an off‐the‐shelf, CD20 × CD3 T‐cell‐engaging bispecific antibody that redirects T cells to eliminate B cells, including those that cause malignant disease [6]. An intravenous (IV) formulation of mosunetuzumab is approved and can be administered in an outpatient setting for the treatment of R/R follicular lymphoma (FL) after ≥ 2 lines of systemic therapy [7, 8]. Polatuzumab vedotin is an antibody‐drug conjugate composed of an anti‐CD79b monoclonal antibody conjugated by a protease‐cleavable linker to a potent microtubule inhibitor, monomethyl auristatin E [3]. Polatuzumab vedotin in combination with chemoimmunotherapy is approved for the treatment of previously untreated and R/R diffuse large B‐cell lymphoma (DLBCL) [9, 10]. Mosunetuzumab IV in combination with polatuzumab vedotin has demonstrated durable responses in patients with R/R LBCL [11].

A subcutaneous (SC) formulation of mosunetuzumab has been developed, with the aim of further improving safety and patient convenience, with reduced administration times. In a pivotal Phase II study, mosunetuzumab SC met the primary endpoint by demonstrating pharmacokinetic noninferiority to mosunetuzumab IV [12]. Mosunetuzumab SC also achieved a high complete response (CR) rate (62%) and durable responses (median duration of CR [DOCR], 34.6 months) alongside a manageable safety profile in patients with R/R FL who had received ≥ 2 lines of prior therapy, and based on the results of the study mosunetuzumab SC has received approvals in this setting [12, 13, 14]. An ongoing Phase Ib/II study (NCT03671018) is evaluating mosunetuzumab (IV or SC) plus polatuzumab vedotin in R/R LBCL [11]. At the primary analysis, the Phase II single‐arm expansion cohort (n = 98) showed a manageable safety profile and durable responses with mosunetuzumab IV plus polatuzumab vedotin [11, 15]. We report efficacy, safety, pharmacokinetic, and pharmacodynamic data from the Phase II randomized portion of the NCT03671018 study evaluating mosunetuzumab SC plus polatuzumab vedotin (Mosun‐Pola) versus rituximab plus polatuzumab vedotin (R‐Pola) in patients with R/R LBCL, with a median follow‐up of over 2 years.

sec.title: Study Design and Participants
sec.p: NCT03671018 is an ongoing, open‐label, Phase Ib/II, multi‐arm study of Mosun‐Pola in patients with B‐cell non‐Hodgkin lymphoma (B‐NHL). To delineate the contribution of mosunetuzumab to the Mosun‐Pola combination, we conducted an analysis of the Phase II randomized cohort evaluating Mosun (SC)‐Pola versus R‐Pola in R/R LBCL.

Eligible patients were aged ≥ 18 years with histologically confirmed LBCL (DLBCL not otherwise specified, FL Grade 3b, high‐grade B‐cell lymphoma, or transformed FL), had an Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance status of 0–2, and had relapsed disease or disease that was refractory to ≥ 1 previous line of treatment including an anti‐CD20 therapy. Full inclusion and exclusion criteria are listed in the Supporting Information.

The study was conducted in full conformance with the International Council for Harmonisation E6 guideline for Good Clinical Practice and the principles of the Declaration of Helsinki, or the applicable laws and regulations of the country in which the research was conducted, whichever afforded the greater protection to the individual. Procedures were reviewed and approved by the institutional review board before the study was initiated. All patients provided written informed consent.

sec.title: Study Treatment
sec.p: Patients were randomized 1:1 to receive either Mosun‐Pola or R‐Pola and stratified by number of prior therapies (1 vs. ≥ 2). Patients in the Mosun‐Pola arm received mosunetuzumab SC with step‐up dosing in Cycle (C) 1 (C1 Day [D] 1: 5 mg; C1D8: 45 mg; C1D15: 45 mg; C2D1–C8D1: 45 mg) with no requirement for hospitalization. Polatuzumab vedotin IV was administered at 1.8 mg/kg on D1 of C1–6. Patients in the R‐Pola arm received rituximab IV (375 mg/m2) on D1 of C1–8 and polatuzumab vedotin as described. All treatment cycles were 21 days. Retreatment was permitted in the Mosun‐Pola arm for patients who achieved a CR and where progressive disease (PD) was observed following completion of treatment. Crossover treatment with Mosun‐Pola was permitted in patients in the R‐Pola arm with PD during or at end of treatment (EOT), or stable disease at EOT, with up to 8 cumulative cycles of polatuzumab vedotin. Corticosteroid prophylaxis consisting of 20 mg of dexamethasone (preferred) or 80 mg of methylprednisolone, either IV or orally, was administered prior to each mosunetuzumab dose during C1 and was optional thereafter in patients who did not experience cytokine release syndrome (CRS) in the previous cycle (further details provided in the Supporting Information).

sec.title: Study Outcomes
sec.p: The primary efficacy endpoint was best objective response rate (ORR; defined as CR or partial response at any time) as determined by the independent review committee (IRC) using Lugano 2014 criteria [16]. Patients with missing or no response assessments were classified as nonresponders. Key secondary efficacy endpoints included IRC‐assessed CR rates, duration of response (DOR), DOCR, progression‐free survival (PFS), and overall survival (OS). Key secondary investigator‐assessed efficacy endpoints are reported in the Supporting Information.

Safety and tolerability were assessed by incidence, nature, and severity of adverse events (AEs), and by changes in laboratory parameters. AEs were graded according to the National Cancer Institute Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events (version 5.0). CRS was graded using the American Society for Transplantation and Cellular Therapy consensus criteria [17]. After initiation of study drug, all adverse events were reported until 90 days after the last dose of study drug or the initiation of next anti‐lymphoma treatment, whichever was earlier. Serious events assessed by the investigator as related to prior study drug treatment that occurred beyond 90 days after the last dose of study drug were also reported. The safety‐evaluable population included patients who received any study treatment.

Mosunetuzumab serum concentration was analyzed over time to determine the pharmacokinetic profile of mosunetuzumab. Exploratory pharmacodynamic analyses included assessment of B‐cell depletion and recovery after treatment, and T‐cell activation and margination.

sec.title: Statistical Analysis
sec.p: ORR and CR rates were determined and the corresponding Clopper–Pearson exact 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were calculated for each treatment arm. Approximately 80–160 patients with R/R LBCL were planned to enroll in the Phase II randomized portion of the study (40–80 patients in each treatment arm). This provided a margin of error for the 95% exact Clopper–Pearson CIs for estimation of the true ORR not exceeding ±16.7% and ±11.6%, with 40 and 80 patients in each arm, respectively.

DOCR, DOR, PFS, and OS were analyzed by Kaplan–Meier methodology; patients who did not experience PD, relapse, or death were censored at the date of the last evaluable tumor assessment or at the last date known to be alive for OS. Further details are outlined in the Supporting Information.

sec.title: Patients
sec.p: Between November 5, 2021 and January 9, 2023, 80 patients with R/R LBCL were enrolled to receive Mosun‐Pola (n = 40) or R‐Pola (n = 40); a total of 54 patients (67.5%) were enrolled in the United States (US). One patient in the R‐Pola arm did not receive treatment and was not included in the safety analysis.

Baseline characteristics were generally balanced between the treatment arms and are presented in Table 1. The median (range) number of treatment cycles received was 8.0 (1–8) for mosunetuzumab and 6.0 (1–6) for polatuzumab vedotin in the Mosun‐Pola arm, and 4.0 (1–8) for rituximab and 4.0 (1–6) for polatuzumab vedotin in the R‐Pola arm.

sec.p: At data cutoff (November 15, 2024), 20 (50.0%) patients receiving Mosun‐Pola and 11 (28.2%) patients receiving R‐Pola had completed initial treatment, and 17 (42.5%) and 10 (25.6%) patients, respectively, had discontinued the study (Figure 1). Reasons for study discontinuation were death (n = 14; PD [n = 4], AEs [n = 2], other [n = 8]), subject withdrawal (n = 2), and loss to follow‐up (n = 1) in the Mosun‐Pola arm, and death (n = 9; PD [n = 7], AEs [n = 1], other [n = 1]) and subject withdrawal (n = 1) in the R‐Pola arm.

sec.title: Efficacy
sec.p: Median (range) duration of follow‐up in the Mosun‐Pola and R‐Pola arms was 25.7 (1–35) months and 27.2 (0–34) months, respectively. The primary endpoint of IRC‐assessed best ORR was 77.5% (95% CI: 61.6–89.2) for Mosun‐Pola and 50.0% (95% CI: 33.8–66.2) for R‐Pola (Table 2). The CR rate was 55.0% (95% CI: 38.5–70.7) for Mosun‐Pola and 35.0% (95% CI: 20.6–51.7) for R‐Pola. Median DOR and DOCR were not reached in the Mosun‐Pola arm (95% CI: 15.0–not estimable [NE] and 95% CI: 16.8–NE, respectively; Table 2; Figure 2A,B). In the R‐Pola arm, median DOR and DOCR were 11.3 months (95% CI: 5.8–NE) and 12.7 months (95% CI: 3.6–NE), respectively (Table 2; Figure 2A,B).

sec.p: IRC‐assessed median PFS was 25.4 months (95% CI: 9.2–NE) for Mosun‐Pola versus 6.4 months (95% CI: 4.7–18.6) for R‐Pola (hazard ratio [HR] 0.47 [95% CI: 0.2–0.9]; Figure 2C). Median OS was not reached with Mosun‐Pola (95% CI: 17.6–NE) versus 25.5 months (95% CI: 16.2–NE) for R‐Pola (HR: 0.78 [95% CI: 0.4–1.5]; Figure 2D). Investigator‐assessed secondary efficacy endpoints are summarized in Table S1.

In patients who received prior CAR T‐cell therapy, IRC‐assessed ORR was 71.4% for Mosun‐Pola and 73.3% for R‐Pola (odds ratio: 0.91; 95% CI: 0.18–4.64; Figure S1). IRC‐assessed median PFS was 9.2 months (95% CI: 3.1–NE) for Mosun‐Pola versus 6.4 (5.0–NE) for R‐Pola (HR: 0.67 [95% CI: 0.2–1.9]). Median DOR was not reached (95% CI: 3.3–NE) in the Mosun‐Pola arm and 5.8 months (95% CI: 3.0–NE) in the R‐Pola arm. In patients who were refractory or experienced early relapse to their first prior therapy, ORR was 68.0% for Mosun‐Pola and 39.3% for R‐Pola (odds ratio: 3.28; 95% CI: 1.06–10.18).

Four patients in the Mosun‐Pola arm were retreated as per protocol. One patient, who maintained an initial CR for 11.6 months, achieved a subsequent CR following 8 cycles of retreatment; this response was ongoing for 5.9 months at the time of data cutoff. Clinical benefit was limited among the other three retreatment patients who had a shorter initial CR (~6 months): one had stable disease, while two experienced PD resulting in early treatment discontinuation.

After a median (range) follow‐up of 18.7 (15.2–NE) months for the 20 patients who crossed over from R‐Pola to Mosun‐Pola, investigator‐assessed ORR was 50.0% (95% CI: 27.2–72.8), the CR rate was 20.0% (95% CI: 5.7–43.7), the median PFS was 4.4 months (95% CI: 3.1–18.3), and the median DOR was 15.7 months (95% CI: 2.8–NE).

Median time to next anti‐lymphoma treatment was not reached in either arm. A total of 15 (37.5%) patients in the Mosun‐Pola arm and 17 (43.6%) patients in the R‐Pola arm received at least one subsequent therapy. In the Mosun‐Pola arm (n = 40), CAR T‐cell therapy and tafasitamab‐based therapy were administered to three (7.5%) and two (5.0%) patients, respectively. In the R‐Pola arm (n = 39), CAR T‐cell therapy, tafasitamab‐based therapy, a bispecific antibody, or autologous stem cell transplant were administered to one (2.6%) patient each.

sec.title: Safety
sec.p: In the safety population (n = 79; Mosun‐Pola, n = 40; R‐Pola, n = 39), AEs of any grade were reported in all patients (100%) in both treatment arms (Table 3). The most commonly (≥ 30%) reported AEs were injection‐site reaction (Mosun‐Pola, 57.5%), diarrhea (Mosun‐Pola, 47.5%; R‐Pola, 33.3%), neutropenia (Mosun‐Pola, 40.0%; R‐Pola, 23.1%), fatigue (Mosun‐Pola, 35.0%; R‐Pola, 30.8%), peripheral neuropathy (Mosun‐Pola, 32.5%; R‐Pola, 35.9%), constipation (Mosun‐Pola, 30.0%; R‐Pola, 15.4%), and nausea (Mosun‐Pola, 25.0%; R‐Pola, 35.9%) (Table S2). Grade ≥ 3 AEs were reported in 60.0% of patients in the Mosun‐Pola arm and in 53.8% in the R‐Pola arm. The most common (≥ 10%) Grade ≥ 3 AEs were neutrophil count decreased/neutropenia (Mosun‐Pola, 32.5%; R‐Pola, 23.1%) and COVID‐19 pneumonia (Mosun‐Pola, 12.5%; R‐Pola, 2.6%). Serious AEs were observed in 32.5% and 25.6% of patients in the Mosun‐Pola and R‐Pola arms, respectively. Grade 5 AEs occurred in 5.0% of patients receiving Mosun‐Pola (COVID‐19 and COVID‐19 pneumonia [n = 1 each]), and in 2.6% of patients receiving R‐Pola (hepatic failure [n = 1]).

sec.p: AEs leading to discontinuation of study treatment occurred in 7.5% (3/40) of patients in the Mosun‐Pola arm (COVID‐19 pneumonia [n = 1], peripheral motor neuropathy [n = 1], peripheral sensory neuropathy [n = 1]) and in 7.7% (3/39) of patients in the R‐Pola arm (peripheral neuropathy [n = 1], neutrophil count decreased [n = 1], pain in extremity [n = 1]); none of which were considered related to mosunetuzumab or rituximab treatment (Table 3). Polatuzumab vedotin‐related AEs that led to discontinuation of study treatment occurred in 5.0% (2/40) of patients in the Mosun‐Pola arm and in 5.1% (2/39) of patients in the R‐Pola arm.

CRS events were reported in five (12.5%) patients in the Mosun‐Pola arm (Grade 1, 10.0%; Grade 2, 2.5%); one CRS event led to hospitalization. All CRS events occurred after the C1D1 dose (Figure 3) with a median (range) time to CRS onset of 2 (1–3) days and a median (range) duration of 2 (1–5) days. Management of CRS included tocilizumab (n = 1; 2.5%) and corticosteroids (n = 1; 2.5%), and all CRS events resolved by data cutoff.

sec.p: Infections were reported in 45.0% and 33.3% of patients in the Mosun‐Pola and R‐Pola arms, respectively, and occurred across C1–8 through the adverse event reporting period (Table 4). Infection AEs considered related to treatment were reported in 17.5% and 2.6% of patients in the Mosun‐Pola and R‐Pola arms, respectively, and serious infections occurred in 22.5% and 17.9% of patients, respectively. COVID‐19 was the most commonly (≥ 10%) reported AE of infection. Overall, 27.5% of patients in the Mosun‐Pola arm and 25.6% in the R‐Pola arm had confirmed or suspected COVID‐19/COVID‐19 pneumonia. Three patients in the Mosun‐Pola arm had hypogammaglobulinemia reported as an AE (Grade 2: 5%; Grade 3: 2.5%), and there were no reported cases in the R‐Pola arm. Five patients in the Mosun‐Pola arm and two patients in the R‐Pola arm received IVIG for prophylaxis or treatment.

sec.p: There were no investigator‐reported events of immune effector‐cell associated neurotoxicity syndrome in either treatment arm (Table 4). In total, 57.5% of patients treated with Mosun‐Pola reported injection‐site reactions (Grade 1: 37.5%; Grade 2: 20.0%). Neutropenia occurred in 40.0% of patients who received Mosun‐Pola (Grade 2: 7.5%; Grade 3: 17.5%; Grade 4: 15.0%) and none of these events were considered to be serious; one patient experienced a Grade 3 event of febrile neutropenia. Neutropenia was reported in 23.1% of patients treated with R‐Pola and febrile neutropenia was not observed. In the Mosun‐Pola and R‐Pola treatment arms, peripheral neuropathy occurred in 32.5% (Grade 1: 20.0%; Grade 2: 12.5%) and 35.9% (Grade 1: 17.9%; Grade 2: 15.4%; Grade 3: 2.6%; Table 4) of patients, of whom 11/40 (27.5%) and 11/39 (28.2%) experienced events that were considered related to Mosun‐Pola and R‐Pola, respectively.

For the 20 patients who crossed over from R‐Pola to Mosun‐Pola, the safety profile was consistent with patients who received initial treatment with Mosun‐Pola. AEs of any grade were reported in 85.0% of patients, serious AEs in 25.0%, and Grade 5 AEs in 5.0%. One patient experienced Grade 1 CRS.

sec.title: Pharmacokinetics
sec.p: The pharmacokinetic profile of Mosun‐Pola was comparable with that of single‐agent mosunetuzumab (Figure S2) [18].

sec.title: Pharmacodynamics
sec.p: B‐cell depletion in the Mosun‐Pola arm occurred by C2 and was sustained throughout treatment, with B‐cell recovery subsequently observed in most patients (58% [11/19] recovered to ≥ 70 cells/μl) by 12–15 months after treatment completion (Figure S3A). Parallel analysis of natural killer (NK) cells and T cells demonstrated sustained levels with Mosun‐Pola, with a trend toward immune‐cell recovery after treatment completion. CD4 cells were decreased at treatment initiation and recovered to lower levels within the normal range post treatment; CD8 levels remained at normal levels throughout treatment and after treatment completion (Figure S3B).

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: In this Phase II study Mosun (SC)‐Pola administered as a fixed‐duration outpatient regimen demonstrated high efficacy and promising durability compared with R‐Pola, while maintaining a manageable safety profile in patients with R/R LBCL. Despite enrolling patients mainly from the US, results from the Mosun‐Pola cohort of this study were similar to those observed in the global Phase III SUNMO study (NCT05171647), which compared Mosun (SC)‐Pola with rituximab plus gemcitabine‐oxaliplatin (GemOx) in patients with R/R LBCL [19]. These data are also the first to demonstrate that the combined effect of a CD20 × CD3 bispecific antibody, mosunetuzumab SC, with an antibody drug conjugate, polatuzumab vedotin, is superior to R‐Pola, a common bridging therapy to CAR T cells for patients with R/R LBCL.

Mosun‐Pola demonstrated favorable efficacy with high IRC‐assessed ORR and CR rates of 78% and 55%, respectively, compared with R‐Pola (ORR, 50%; CR, 35%); ORRs were consistent across patient subgroups (prior CAR T‐cell therapy, 71%; primary refractory/early relapse, 68%) although the sample sizes are small and should be interpreted with caution. With a median follow‐up of over 2 years, median IRC‐assessed PFS with Mosun‐Pola was increased by a factor of four compared with R‐Pola (25.4 months vs. 6.4 months) and median DOCR and OS were not reached. These results are particularly promising given the high‐risk disease profile of the patients enrolled in the study, 36% of whom had received prior CAR T‐cell therapy.

In patients with PD or those who did not have adequate responses to R‐Pola, clinical benefit (ORR, 50%) was observed after receiving crossover treatment with Mosun‐Pola. Responses in these patients were durable (median DOR, 15.7 months), indicating that the T‐cell redirecting activity of mosunetuzumab can overcome resistance mechanisms associated with prior anti‐CD20 and anti‐CD79b therapies.

Although cross‐trial comparisons should be interpreted with caution due to differences in patient population and study design, studies of bispecific antibody monotherapies have reported response rates of 24%–63% in patients with R/R LBCL after ≥ 2 lines of therapy with a median PFS of 3.2–4.9 months [20, 21, 22, 23]. In early phase studies, lower CR rates have been observed with mosunetuzumab IV (24%) in patients with R/R DLBCL [23] and with polatuzumab vedotin (16%) [24] monotherapy in patients with R/R B‐NHL, suggesting potential synergistic activity of the Mosun‐Pola combination. The response rate and durable efficacy of Mosun‐Pola is also encouraging when compared with available treatments for R/R LBCL. When used in the second‐line or later setting, polatuzumab vedotin plus bendamustine and rituximab achieved a best ORR of 63% and a median PFS of 9.2 months [25], and tafasitamab plus lenalidomide achieved an ORR of 58% and a median PFS of 11.6 months [26]. Among studies evaluating CAR T‐cell therapy as second‐ or third‐line treatment in both transplant‐eligible and transplant‐ineligible patients, best ORR of 52%–92% and a median PFS of 6.8–14.7 months have been reported [27, 28, 29, 30, 31, 32]. However, complicated administration logistics and potentially severe toxicities often limit the accessibility of CAR T‐cell therapy for patients [4]. Other bispecific combination therapies, including glofitamab plus GemOx (best ORR: 68%) and epcoritamab plus GemOx (best ORR: 85%), have also shown promising efficacy in this setting [33, 34, 35, 36]. However, it is important to note that the Mosun‐Pola regimen has the advantage of not containing a conventional chemotherapy backbone.

The overall safety profile of Mosun‐Pola was comparable with that reported for mosunetuzumab and polatuzumab vedotin administered as monotherapies in patients with R/R B‐NHL [23, 24], and no new safety signals were identified, supporting the outpatient use of this treatment regimen. AEs leading to Mosun‐Pola treatment discontinuation were reported in 7.5% of patients. The incidence of CRS was 12.5% with no Grade ≥ 3 events; all CRS events were confined to the first treatment cycle and resolved by data cutoff. Tocilizumab and corticosteroids were administered to one patient each. The observed incidence and severity of CRS events with Mosun‐Pola were lower than that previously reported for mosunetuzumab monotherapy (any grade: 26%; Grade 3: 2.3%) [23] and compare favorably with that reported in pivotal studies involving other T‐cell engaging therapies for LBCL (axicabtagene ciloleucel: 92%/6%; lisocabtagene maraleucel: 49%/1%; glofitamab: 63%/4%; epcoritamab: 50%/3%) [20, 21, 29, 30]. Infection AEs with Mosun‐Pola were mainly low grade and manageable across both treatment arms (Grade ≥ 3: 20.0% for Mosun‐Pola and 15.4% for R‐Pola), and the Grade ≥ 3 rates were similar to those observed with other T‐cell engaging therapies (axicabtagene ciloleucel: 14%; lisocabtagene maraleucel: 15%; glofitamab: 15%; epcoritamab: 16%) [20, 21, 29, 30]. Overall, subcutaneous administration of mosunetuzumab and outpatient use of this regimen, with the lowest CRS rate among all T‐cell‐based regimens, favor Mosun‐Pola for community adoption.

Exploratory analyses demonstrating B‐cell recovery after treatment completion substantiate the use of mosunetuzumab SC as a fixed‐duration regimen in combination with polatuzumab vedotin. Both B and T cells (particularly CD4+) were below the normal range at study enrollment, likely due to prior treatment. While B cells were depleted during treatment, T cells were maintained and both immune subsets recovered to the normal range following treatment completion. In contrast to T and B cells, NK cells were consistently observed within the normal range prior to, during, and post treatment. Collectively, while the pharmacodynamics are unique to each subset, the peripheral immune profile appears to normalize post treatment.

Strengths of the study include the randomized design that aimed to provide further insight into understanding the potential synergy or superior efficacy of Mosun‐Pola versus R‐Pola in a controlled setting. Other strengths include the high‐risk patient population, including patients who relapsed following CAR T‐cell therapy, and the low rates of CRS events in comparison with other bispecific antibody pivotal studies. Limitations of the study include the small sample size and the crossover design, which may have impacted observations of OS benefit. While investigating single‐agent polatuzumab vedotin would have provided a clearer analysis of the contribution of mosunetuzumab to the combination's efficacy, R‐Pola provides a more clinically rational control, and ultimately, the superiority of Mosun‐Pola compared with R‐Pola supports the additive therapeutic benefit of mosunetuzumab.

This Phase II study offers a deeper understanding of the Mosun (SC)‐Pola regimen, providing extended follow‐up, additional safety data, and identifies the added benefit of the combination over polatuzumab vedotin alone. Notably, this study enrolled a mainly US population, including in academic and community settings, supporting the applicability of this regimen to this region. The efficacy and safety results observed with Mosun‐Pola are consistent with the global Phase III SUNMO study (NCT05171647) [19].

In conclusion, fixed‐duration mosunetuzumab SC combined with polatuzumab vedotin demonstrated superior efficacy with durable responses compared with R‐Pola, with over 2 years median follow‐up. The outpatient use of Mosun‐Pola was supported by a manageable safety profile. Results from this study demonstrate the sustained benefit of Mosun‐Pola for patients with R/R LBCL and findings are consistent with the promising results observed in the global Phase III SUNMO study.
